node.label: Ian McKay
node.date_label: Tartanism Triumphant 1992 · The Quest of the Folk 1994 · 'A Note on Region' and the liberal order prospectus 2000 · later readings 2005, 2008, 2009 · coverage through 2000
node.description: Reads twentieth-century Nova Scotia's 'folk' as a cultural selection by folklorists, handicraft planners, writers and the tourist state, and as a local version of an international antimodernist wave (1992, 1994). In 2000 he proposed treating Canada as a project of liberal rule, to be studied through the implantation of liberalism across a heterogeneous terrain, and asked how 'region' fits that project. Later work turns to the Canadian left as a counter-project (2005, 2008) and answers the framework's critics (2009).
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ian McKay (b. 1953); “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954” (1992); The Quest of the Folk: Antimodernism and Cultural Selection in Twentieth-Century Nova Scotia (1994); “A Note on ‘Region’ in Writing the History of Atlantic Canada” (2000); “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History” (2000). Later readings: Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005); Reasoning Otherwise (2008); “Canada as a Long Liberal Revolution” (2009).
node.scope_note: This entry presents the 1992 article and the 1994 book on antimodernism and the folk, and the two essays of 2000 on region and liberal order. The 1992 article is read at pp. 5–9 and 13–14; the 1994 book is checked at summary and contents level, with its closing argument (p. 306) quoted by Muise (1998); the region essay is read in full; the prospectus is checked at abstract level, with pp. 620–21 quoted by Fecteau (2009). The framework takes its name from his prospectus, but state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it and commentators name Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources; he is not presented as the founder of a field. The 2005, 2008 and 2009 works are later readings.

proposed_edges.relationship: Canada as a project of liberal rule: the prospectus of 2000
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (2000). The prospectus abstract (read) proposes mapping 'the Canadian state as a project of liberal rule in northern North America' to get beyond the 'socio-cultural versus national-political impasse'. Its core formulation (pp. 620–21) is checked as quoted by Fecteau (2009): 'Canada-as-project can be analyzed through the study of the implantation and expansion over a heterogeneous terrain of a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism.' The prospectus body is not read here. McKay's spring 2000 Acadiensis essay (pp. 90–91, read) sets out the same programme in his own words: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; the project 'was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. A contribution, not a founding: state-formation studies (Curtis 1988; Greer and Radforth 1992) precede it, and Pâquet (2009) names Gramsci and Fernande Roy (1988) as its sources. In the sampled corpus, 90 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the prospectus. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. The 2009 reply and the histories of the left (2005, 2008) are later readings, not evidence for this edge.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The prospectus strand ('Canada as a project of liberal rule') holds McKay and lof_mckay_2000 and is exactly the checked claim. property_and_capitalism and debate_2009 rest on the 2009 reply, which is a later reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Antimodernism and the invented folk in twentieth-century Nova Scotia (1992, 1994)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1992, 1994). In 'Tartanism Triumphant' (Acadiensis, 1992; pp. 5–9 read) McKay asks how Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century, when 'a collection of hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. His broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9); the narrow answer is the state's cultural power under Angus L. Macdonald. Note 12 takes Lears's definition of American antimodernism and adds the 'simple life' and 'nature'. The Quest of the Folk (1994) is checked at summary and contents level: chapters on 'The Idea of the Folk', Helen Creighton and folklore, Mary Black and handicrafts, the simple life, and the folk 'under conditions of postmodernity'. Muise's review essay (Acadiensis, 1998; pp. 128–32 read) describes the three case studies and quotes the book's conclusion that 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics' (p. 306). Wright's 1995 Acadiensis review essay on English-Canadian intellectual history cites the book for 'a very skilled handling of Antonio Gramsci's theory of cultural hegemony by an historian' (p. 132 n. 29). A contribution to the field's cultural strand, not its origin: Berger, McKillop and Owram precede it. In the sampled corpus, 56 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the book. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence. In the Province of History (2010, with Bates) is a later reading.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: antimodernism_folk ('Antimodernism and the invented folk') holds McKay, cic_mckay_1994 and the Lears comparison; the 1992 article's n. 12 is McKay's own checked use of Lears.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rethinking 'region' inside a history of the liberal project (2000)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence (Acadiensis, spring 2000; pp. 89–101 read; a lightly edited version of a talk prepared for the August 1997 Atlantic Canada Workshop, dated here by publication). McKay finds that the 1990s 'multiplication of subject-positions, epistemologies and methodologies places a question mark over the very concept of an "Atlantic Canada"' (p. 90). He then asks where region fits a history of Canada as a liberal project and answers 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). He sets aside natural, essentialist definitions of the region (pp. 95–96); he finds heartland–hinterland and dependency models descriptively rich, but asks them to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99). He would resist a nationalizing historiography that reduces the region to one inferior term (p. 99). As an agenda he proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and a regional 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). He also rejects the charge that regionalists are a 'balkanizing faction' (p. 91). This is a reconsideration from inside the field. In the sampled corpus, 4 of 1,303 strict History doctoral dissertations dated 2009–2026 cite the essay under its main record (one more under a variant record).
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: questioning_region holds McKay (2000), Friesen (2000) and Buckner (2000). Kind: the roster row calls him a critic. The essay criticizes three ways of defining region but defends the concept and proposes an agenda for it, so contribution is the closer reading. If reviewers prefer critique, it should point at a strand for the specific positions criticized (dependency or heartland–hinterland models), not at the field as a whole. No such strand exists at 1.128, so the draft does not propose one. Optional because the PhD trace is small and edge_814 (cdn_regional → who_killed_debate) already places regional history in the debate.

new_sources.title: Ian McKay, “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954,” Acadiensis 21, no. 2 (Spring 1992): 5–47.
new_sources.citation: Ian McKay, “Tartanism Triumphant: The Construction of Scottishness in Nova Scotia, 1933–1954,” Acadiensis 21, no. 2 (Spring 1992): 5–47.

verification.note: PDF citation line on p. 5: Acadiensis XXI, 2 (Spring 1992), pp. 5–47; author line Ian McKay. Pages 5–9 read closely, with notes 1–13. Nova Scotia 'became Scottish' in the second quarter of the twentieth century; 'hazy generalizations and ethnic stereotypes' became 'a natural and obvious "commonsense"'. Broad answer: 'it was part of an international anti-modernist wave, a local version of a general middle-class search for something outside and better than the crisis-ridden modern world it inhabited' (pp. 8–9). Narrow answer: Premier Angus L. Macdonald 'used the state's cultural power' to fuse a romantic, essentialist Scottishness with tourism (p. 9). Note 12 (p. 9) quotes Lears's definition of American antimodernism (No Place of Grace, p. xv) and adds 'and, I would also add, in the "simple life" and in "nature"'. Pages 13–14 and note 32 also read: the concept of 'invented tradition' is useful 'provided it is acknowledged that all traditions are historically constructed', and Trevor-Roper is said to rely on 'a naive historical realism'. Note 1: a revised version of a paper given to the CHA in 1990. The rest of the article was searched by keyword only, not read. Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/11913; PDF download 11913/12757).

new_sources.scope_note: McKay's own in-period statement of antimodernism as the frame for Nova Scotia's invented identity; his checked use of Lears.

new_sources.citation: D. A. Muise, “Who Owns History Anyway? Reinventing Atlantic Canada for Pleasure and Profit,” Acadiensis 27, no. 2 (Spring 1998): 124–34.

verification.note: Review essay; PDF citation line on p. 124 and signature 'D. A. MUISE'. Pages 124 and 128–32 read (the section on The Quest of the Folk). Muise writes that the book 'examines the origins of the essentialist folk tradition' and that McKay 'explodes the central place of the "folk" in understanding Nova Scotia's culture and history'. He describes three case studies (Helen Creighton, Mary Black and handicrafts, and literary producers including the Song Fishermen) and an afterword, 'The Folk under Conditions of Postmodernity'. McKay acknowledges a debt to Whisnant and Raymond Williams and places himself 'within a neo-marxist framework associated with the work of Antonio Gramsci'. Muise quotes the book (p. 306): 'the concept of the Folk was and remains a powerful obstacle to the formation of a counter-hegemonic cultural politics, without which a new, profoundly emancipatory politics of class, gender and racial equality is inconceivable.' Note 9 lists McKay's earlier essays on the theme (1988, 1992, 1993). Pages 125–27 not read; pp. 133–34 only glanced at (to the signature). Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (article/view/10846; PDF 10846/11670).

source_addenda.cdng_mckay_2000_region: Addendum 2026-10-13 (Claude): the whole essay (pp. 89–101) read in the UNB PDF. Note 1 (p. 89): 'a lightly-edited version of the introductory talk I prepared for the Atlantic Canada Workshop which met in Halifax in August 1997'. Pages 90–91 state the liberal-order programme: 'a strategy of reconnaissance'; 'That project, very briefly, was the project of liberal order, a coherent attempt to install a liberal public philosophy and practice of "peace, order and good government" in northern North America'; 'Canada was thus a process, not a self-evident thing, and the key to this process was liberalization'. Where region fits that approach: 'Quite centrally' (p. 95). The essay sets aside natural and essentialist definitions (pp. 95–96), asks heartland–hinterland and dependency models to 'undergo the rigorous analysis of concepts' (pp. 96–99) and resists a nationalizing historiography (p. 99). It proposes exploring 'the remarkable extent to which Atlantic Canadians built the Canadian liberal project' (p. 99) and the region's 'communitarian critique of the liberal order' (p. 100). Page 89 names 'the Gramscian assumptions that have shaped my outlook'.
